items.title: Can Agentic AI Investigate a Phishing Campaign? Evidence Walkthrough
items.summary: Yes, with a human signing off. An agentic AI can run most of a phishing investigation on its own. It can pull domain registration records, open the lure safely, pivot to related infrastructure, extract indicators and write up a verdict with the evidence attached. What it shouldn't do yet is act on that verdict unchecked, because attackers are already hiding instructions inside phishing emails meant for the AI doing the reading. The evidence for both halves of that answer is now public. Microsoft's randomized trial of 167 security analysts found that its phishing triage agent made them faster and more accurate. Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that one phishing email can carry a lure for the human and a hidden prompt for the AI in the same message. This post walks through what an agentic investigation of a real phishing campaign looks like, evidence item by evidence item, using the lookalike Microsoft Teams domains that researcher Steven Lim exposed in October. Then it covers where agents break, and what to ask before you trust one. What is an agentic AI security investigation? An agentic AI security investigation is one where an AI agent plans and runs the investigation itself. It decides which data sources to query, calls the tools, reads what comes back, chooses the next step and stops when it can support a verdict with evidence a human can check. The phrase "agentic AI security" also gets used for protecting AI agents from attack. This post is about the other direction: agents doing the investigating. The difference from older automation is who picks the next step. A SOAR playbook runs the same steps every time. A chat assistant answers the question an analyst types. An agent sets its own path based on what it finds, which is exactly what makes it useful and exactly what makes it attackable. SOAR playbook AI chat assistant AI investigation agent Who picks the next step The playbook author, in advance The analyst, one prompt at a time The agent, based on each result What it produces Enrichment fields and tickets Answers and summaries A verdict with an evidence trail Typical failure Breaks on anything off-script Only as good as the questions asked Can be steered by content it reads What the evidence says so far The best public data comes from Microsoft. In November 2025, Microsoft economist James Bono published a randomized controlled trial of the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent. Microsoft recruited 167 professional security analysts and split them into groups that triaged a 25-email queue of real, privacy-vetted user-reported emails, 20% of them malicious, with or without the agent. Analysts working with the agent found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute and were up to 77% more accurate, measured by F1 score. They also spent 53% more time on the malicious emails. The paper found no sign they simply rubber-stamped the agent's calls. Read the fine print before quoting those numbers in a budget meeting. Microsoft studied its own product. On the test corpus, the agent's precision and recall were both 100%, which no production deployment should expect, and the paper's own scenario with a less accurate agent and more malicious mail cut the accuracy gain to 48%. The trial also measured triage: one reported email, one verdict. Investigating a campaign means connecting dozens of artifacts across days, and no comparable trial covers that yet. The skeptical data point comes from Gartner. In June 2025, Gartner predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 over costs, unclear value or weak risk controls. It estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI offer real agentic capabilities, calling the rest "agent washing." Put together: agents have measurable value on narrow, high-volume phishing work, and plenty of products wearing the label won't deliver it. The way to tell them apart is to watch one work a real case. Evidence walkthrough: investigating the fake Teams portals In October 2026, Microsoft Security MVP Steven Lim posted a series of lookalike Microsoft Teams domains on LinkedIn, with screenshots. They make a good test case because the attack never needed a phishing email, so an inbox-only investigation would have missed most of it. Below is the evidence chain an investigation agent should build from that same starting point, one step at a time. It reconstructs the work from the artifacts Lim made public; it is not output from a specific product run. Each step names what the agent does, what it collects and where a human should check. Step 1: Enrich the seed domain The seed is teams-online[.]com. The agent pulls registration data and reputation in parallel. Lim's screenshot gives the answers: registered Oct. 4, 2026, through a privacy service attached to the registrar Global Domain Group, and no active verdict in Microsoft Defender threat intelligence. A lazy agent stops here and calls the domain clean. A good one treats "no verdict" on a four-day-old domain as missing data, not a pass, and weighs what it does know: brand name in the domain, days old, owner hidden. Human check: none yet. This is enrichment, and it's cheap to be wrong here. Step 2: Render the page safely and compare it to the real thing The agent opens the URL in an isolated browser and captures a screenshot, the page source and the assets it loads. The page is a near-copy of the Teams pre-join screen: camera preview, audio options, a "Meeting with the Design team" heading, Sign in and Need help links. The evidence that matters is the comparison. The agent should record which brand assets appear, how closely the layout matches the real join page and whether the page asks for anything (a name, credentials, a download). Human check: confirm the brand match. Visual similarity scoring can flag a legitimate partner page that embeds a Teams meeting. Step 3: Pivot to sibling infrastructure One domain is an incident. Several are a campaign. The agent searches for domains that share traits with the seed: the "teams-" plus generic-word naming pattern, the registrar, hosting, TLS certificates and page templates. Lim's later posts surface two siblings. teams-livemeeting[.]com shared the registrar Global Domain Group, was about 15 days old and was flagged by 3 of 92 vendors in a domain scan. teams-cloud[.]live copied the same Teams join page and was five days old. This is where agents most often overreach. A registrar serves many unrelated customers, so a shared registrar alone proves little. A careful agent links siblings on stronger evidence, such as shared IP addresses, certificate details, identical page code or tracking IDs, and labels each link with its confidence. Lim describes the domains as registered by the same organization; the agent should attribute that claim to him until its own evidence supports it. Human check: review every link the agent marks as "same actor" before anyone writes that in a report. Step 4: Trace how victims reach the pages An email-centered workflow looks for the message that delivered the link. Here there may be no message. Lim reported that teams-livemeeting[.]com surfaced through sponsored search ads and an AI-generated answer, and his screenshot shows a search engine's AI overview citing it beside Microsoft's own links. A later post shows teams-cloud[.]live ranking second in ordinary results for "teams cloud live." The agent should capture these delivery paths as evidence too: the search queries, the ad or result position and the date seen. For practitioners, this maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1583.001 (acquiring domains) and T1608.006 (SEO poisoning). Human check: none for collection. The findings feed the response plan. Step 5: Follow the payload path without detonating blindly On teams-cloud[.]live, joining the meeting led to a fake "You need to update Microsoft Teams" prompt. The Update Teams button downloaded a file named realtek-demo.txt. The agent records the filename, hash and file type, and notes that a text file can't execute on its own. The honest verdict is "staged lure, payload not yet weaponized or swapped per visitor," not "malware delivery." Overstating this step is how investigation reports lose credibility. Human check: decide whether to detonate further, for example by revisiting from a different region or browser profile, since some kits serve payloads selectively. Step 6: Write the verdict and the response plan The output should be a verdict a person can audit in five minutes: three lookalike Teams domains, cloned join pages, delivery through search and ads, a staged fake update, and a confidence level for each claim. The response plan follows from the evidence: block the domains in DNS and web filtering, which is what Lim advised; search proxy and DNS logs for any visits from your users; file takedown requests with the registrar and host; and add the naming pattern to watch lists. Human check: approve every action that touches production or goes outside the company. Blocks are reversible. A takedown request filed under your company's name is not. The evidence ledger This is what the finished case file should contain, and what you should expect any agent to show you. That is the core weakness, and attackers have already found it. Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that phishing emails in one campaign carried a password-protected attachment for the human and hidden instructions for the AI assistant that summarizes the inbox. Sublime Security documented phishing emails stuffed with invisible text copied from real Adidas newsletters and romance novels, meant to push AI filters toward a benign verdict. StrongestLayer found a malicious file carrying an "LLM_IGNORE_START" comment aimed at AI scanners. Sublime's researchers put the hidden-text technique at under 1% of phishing traffic, so this is early. It is also exactly the input an investigation agent consumes. Three other failure modes show up in practice: Overconfident links. Step 3 is where agents turn a shared registrar into "the same threat actor." A claim without an evidence item behind it should never reach a report. Missing business context. An agent doesn't know that your marketing team runs a microsite on a hyphenated domain, or which vendor portals your staff use. Too much permission. An agent that can file takedowns or change firewall rules on its own turns one poisoned page into an outage or a legal letter. The defenses are design choices you can ask about. Treat everything the agent fetches as data, never as instructions. Separate the permission to read from the permission to act. Require every claim in a verdict to point to an evidence item. Log every tool call so the investigation can be replayed. Keep a human approval step on anything that leaves the building. Seven questions to ask before you trust an investigation agent Gartner's agent-washing estimate means most demos will look impressive. These questions separate an agent that investigates from a chatbot with a playbook behind it. Show me the evidence ledger for a real case. Every claim in the verdict should link to an artifact: a record, a screenshot, a log line. What does it do with a domain that has no reputation yet? If the answer is "marks it clean," it would have passed teams-online[.]com. Can it investigate beyond the inbox? Lookalike domain registrations, search results and ads are delivery channels now. An email-only agent sees part of the campaign. How does it separate content from instructions? Ask what happens when a phishing page or email contains hidden text addressed to the AI. What can it do without human approval? Get the list in writing. Read-only enrichment can be automatic. Blocks, takedowns and user notifications need a person. Can we replay an investigation? You need every query and tool call logged, so an analyst or auditor can retrace the path. What is its accuracy on our data? Vendor benchmarks are best cases; in Microsoft's trial, the agent was 100% accurate on the test corpus. Run a pilot on your own reported phishing and measure false positives and misses yourself. Frequently asked questions Can AI agents investigate phishing on their own? AI agents can gather and correlate most of the evidence in a phishing investigation on their own, including domain records, page captures, related infrastructure and indicators. They should not take outward-facing actions such as takedowns or blocks without human approval, because attackers can plant instructions in the content agents read. How accurate are AI phishing triage agents? In Microsoft's randomized trial with 167 analysts, people working with the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent were up to 77% more accurate and found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute. The agent was 100% accurate on that test corpus, so expect lower numbers in production and measure on your own data. Is agentic AI different from SOAR for phishing response? Yes. A SOAR playbook runs fixed steps written in advance. An AI agent chooses its next step based on what it finds, so it can follow a lead like a sibling domain that no playbook anticipated. That flexibility is also why agents need evidence logging and approval controls. What is the biggest risk of AI agents in security investigations? Prompt injection. An investigation agent reads attacker-controlled emails and web pages, and researchers at Barracuda, Sublime Security and StrongestLayer have documented phishing content with hidden text aimed at AI systems. The fix is design: treat fetched content as data, limit what the agent can do without approval and log every step. Will AI investigation agents replace SOC analysts? The evidence points to a shift in analyst work rather than replacement. In Microsoft's trial, analysts with the agent spent 53% more time on the malicious emails, because the agent handled sorting and first-pass reasoning. Judgment calls on attribution, business context and response still sat with people. Watch an agent work a real case The fake Teams portals show where investigation work has moved. The evidence sat in domain registrations, cloned pages, search results and an AI answer. An agent that only reads the inbox would have seen a fraction of it, and an agent that can't show its evidence shouldn't be trusted with the rest. Cyble describes Blaze as correlating threat intelligence and digital risk signals, extracting indicators, and producing decisions that are explainable and auditable. items.title: Apache Patches Critical HTTP/2 Flaw Allowing Remote Code Execution on Web Servers
items.summary: Apache has fixed a critical bug in its HTTP/2 module that could let a remote attacker run code on a web server. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-119618 and affects mod_http2. The fix came on November 11, 2026, in Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71. The bug sits in a function called assign_headers(). Apache says it is a concurrency problem, where shared resources are used without proper locking. Put simply, two parts of the code can touch the same piece of memory at the same time. That can damage the heap, the memory area a program uses while it runs, and this can lead to remote code execution. Apache’s own impact scale reserves the “Critical” label for bugs that a remote attacker could use to run code on a server. These are the kind of bugs that could spread on their own, like a worm. The CVE entry is still marked as reserved, so there is no public CVSS score or detailed technical write-up yet. Admins should not wait for those details before patching. Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 are affected. People who run the standalone mod_h2 from GitHub should check versions 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Servers that serve HTTP/2 traffic are the main concern, since the flaw lives in that module. Anthropic’s OSS Scanner found the flaw and reported it to the Apache security team on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it on their own on November 3. Apache Patches Critical HTTP/2 Flaw Apache released the fix on November 11, about two weeks after the first report. Two teams finding the same bug within days shows how much attention researchers are giving HTTP/2 code. The same release closes two more holes. CVE-2026-106023 is rated “important” and sits in mod_md. A NULL pointer error there can crash a child process while it handles a request, and it affects versions 2.4.30 through 2.4.70. CVE-2026-109163 is a “low” rated one-byte stack overflow in mod_vhost_alias. It affects only versions 2.4.69 and 2.4.70. This is part of a long run of Apache fixes this year. Version 2.4.69 in October fixed 20 CVEs, and 2.4.68 in June fixed 13. Cyber Security News covered the October update in its report on multiple Apache HTTP Server flaws that could enable code execution. HTTP/2 has been a weak spot too. In June, the “HTTP/2 Bomb” denial-of-service exploit hit the default HTTP/2 setups of several popular web servers, including Apache. Many admins who patched in October now have to patch again, only weeks later. That is tiring, but this bug is serious enough to justify it. The best step is to upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 as soon as you can. Start with public-facing servers that have HTTP/2 turned on. Apache has fixed a critical bug in its HTTP/2 module that could let a remote attacker run code on a web server. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-119618 and affects mod_http2. The fix came on November 11, 2026, in Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71.

The bug sits in a function called assign_headers(). Apache says it is a concurrency problem, where shared resources are used without proper locking.

Put simply, two parts of the code can touch the same piece of memory at the same time. That can damage the heap, the memory area a program uses while it runs, and this can lead to remote code execution.

Apache’s own impact scale reserves the “Critical” label for bugs that a remote attacker could use to run code on a server. These are the kind of bugs that could spread on their own, like a worm.

The CVE entry is still marked as reserved, so there is no public CVSS score or detailed technical write-up yet. Admins should not wait for those details before patching.

Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 are affected. People who run the standalone mod_h2 from GitHub should check versions 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Servers that serve HTTP/2 traffic are the main concern, since the flaw lives in that module.

Anthropic’s OSS Scanner found the flaw and reported it to the Apache security team on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it on their own on November 3.

items.title: Hackers Hijack ConnectWise ScreenConnect to Deploy SCKit Malware Across 288 Devices at 48 Organizations
items.summary: Attackers have taken over cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels and used them to push a custom toolkit called SCKit to at least 288 managed devices across 48 organizations. Security firm Huntress first saw the activity on November 11, 2026, and says all 288 hosts were hit within about 90 minutes. Huntress reports that about one third of them were hit in the first 10 minutes. The attacker used the Run command feature in the ScreenConnect panel to send commands to many endpoints at once. These commands ran with SYSTEM rights, which is the highest level on Windows. The command first checked for an existing ScreenConnect client. It then downloaded a rogue installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi and installed it silently. Huntress says it is working with ConnectWise on the case. Reports say the latest ScreenConnect versions, 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, are affected. ConnectWise says it has found no sign that its own systems were broken into and no flaw in ScreenConnect itself. ConnectWise ScreenConnect Hijacked In a public advisory posted on November 11, ConnectWise named five outside extensions that may be tied to the activity. These are Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link. The company turned them off in about 400 partner environments as a safety step. ConnectWise says these extensions offer an API that can run remote commands, and a passphrase set by the partner protects that API. Having an extension installed does not prove a break-in. The company has not yet found the first point of entry or the full scope. Partners who run servers on their own premises must turn the extensions off themselves, because ConnectWise cannot do it for them. SCKit is a package of 16 files, including PowerShell scripts, batch files, and settings data. The infected machine sends its Windows ID to the attacker’s server. The server replies with the key needed to unlock a payload made for that one machine. This makes file hashes a weak way to spot the threat. Next, the scripts install a second rogue ScreenConnect client and add exclusions to Microsoft Defender. They also create a tool called RelayTrap in C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap . A scheduled task named TrapWatch stops the real ScreenConnect client and puts the attacker’s copy in its place. The machine still looks normal to the admin. Huntress also noted that the C# code for RelayTrap looks like it was written with an AI model. The toolkit has a second goal. Huntress found code built to wait until a technician connects to an infected device. It then pulls a dropper onto the technician’s workstation and steals the .aspxauth session cookie. With that cookie, the code tries to reach every other session the technician can open, and it uploads a payload to the panel’s Shared Toolbox. Huntress has not seen this spread work. The console takeover failed in every host log it has checked so far. Still, the design shows why defenders should be careful. This is not the first time criminals have turned ScreenConnect against its users. In September, Cyber Security News covered worm-like rogue ScreenConnect clients that passed staged scripts between Windows machines. Around the same time, CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. That flaw allows file transfers during a live session without the host’s approval. Huntress says ConnectWise later fixed it, and it scored 9.9 on the CVSS scale. Huntress and ConnectWise give the same core advice. Do not connect to a suspect machine through ScreenConnect, because that session can carry the malware to your own workstation. Use EDR live response, WinRM, or another tool outside ScreenConnect. Teams should also: Isolate affected hosts until cleanup is finished. Huntress saw some machines reinfect after isolation was lifted. Remove the rogue client, the TrapWatch task, the RelayTrap folder, and the RelayTrapLiteAlert Run key. Check Run Command and Toolbox history for jobs nobody started. Revoke active web sessions and rotate credentials from a clean device. Indicators include the domains newnewnew.gotdns[.]org , soxnewwork.homedns[.]org , cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com , and ns.mo7sen[.]dev . They also include the IP address 185.99.255[.]28 and the participant name Addmin . ConnectWise says the investigation is still open and it will update its advisory as facts are confirmed. items.title: Node.js Fixes 16 Security Flaws That Could Expose TLS Private Keys and Crash Servers Remotely
items.summary: The Node.js project has released fixes for 16 security flaws across its 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines. Seven are rated high, six medium, and three low. The official advisory says the patched builds are v22.23.5 , v24.22.3 and v26.13.1 . The update also refreshes three bundled parts: llhttp, undici, and sqlite. Memory Leak Could Expose TLS Private Keys The high-severity flaw is CVE-2026-123864. It affects the HTTPS code in all three lines. A client with no login can read memory that belongs to other connections. That memory can hold TLS private keys and other users’ requests. The cause is a re-entry problem. A zero-length TLS write can make Node.js decrypt the next record while the HTTP parser is still reading a body. This causes a use-after-free and an out-of-bounds read, so the server copies old heap memory into the request body. A server is at risk only if a handler calls res.flushHeaders() early and later ends with a non-empty chunk. A route that echoes or stores request bodies lets the attacker read the leak. Plain node:http is not affected, according to the Node.js security notes . HTTP/2 code accounts for most of the list. CVE-2026-123863 lets any client abort a default HTTP/2 server. It is a variant of CVE-2024-27983 that the older fix missed. CVE-2026-123874 and CVE-2026-123875 hit servers that send files with respondWithFile() . One corrupts memory. The other crashes the server when a download is canceled, and a handful of canceled requests is enough. CVE-2026-123866 can send freed response memory to a peer, which may include other users’ response data. CVE-2026-123865 leaks memory and file descriptors forever once a session fails during shutdown. It repairs a gap left by CVE-2026-48937, which we covered in our June Node.js patch report . Two medium flaws also matter. CVE-2026-123868 lets a client send tiny one-byte frames and make the server keep about 114 bytes for every 10 bytes sent. One stream can then hold hundreds of megabytes. CVE-2026-123828 is a one-byte heap overflow in session.altsvc() that aborts the process when an app passes a long :authority value to it. # CVE Severity Affected Lines Issue 1 CVE-2026-123863 High 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 session teardown assertion lets a remote client abort the server 2 CVE-2026-123864 High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x HTTPS zero-length TLS write re-enters llhttp and leaks heap memory, including TLS private keys 3 CVE-2026-123865 High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 sessions never clean up after a protocol error during shutdown, leaking memory and file descriptors 4 CVE-2026-123866 High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 stream teardown use-after-free sends freed response memory to the peer 5 CVE-2026-126051 High 24.x, 26.x Deferred TLS handshake callbacks cause a remote uncaught exception that kills the server 6 CVE-2026-123872 High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x TLS 1.2 renegotiation lets a client change servername and bypass client certificate checks 7 CVE-2026-123874 High 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 use-after-free in respondWithFile() streams reset during a pending write 8 CVE-2026-123828 Medium 24.x, 26.x One-byte heap overflow in session.altsvc() with a long origin 9 CVE-2026-123867 Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CA-only SNI client-CA override falls back to the default CA, bypassing per-host mTLS 10 CVE-2026-123868 Medium 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 inbound data on an undrained stream escapes maxSessionMemory , allowing memory exhaustion 11 CVE-2026-123871 Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x Proxy credentials exposed in ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG error messages 12 CVE-2026-123877 Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x https.Agent reuses a TLS session across different CA policies, bypassing certificate validation 13 CVE-2026-123875 Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x Cancelling a respondWithFile() download causes a NULL dereference and crashes the server 14 CVE-2026-123829 Low 22.x, 24.x, 26.x Recursive fs.watch leaks names of files the Permission Model denies (macOS and Windows) 15 CVE-2026-123862 Low 22.x, 24.x, 26.x A pending zlib params() plus destroy() throws an uncatchable assertion and ends the process 16 CVE-2026-106071 Low 22.x, 24.x, 26.x Permission Model wildcard lookup over-grants file system access Login and Certificate Checks Failure Several bugs weaken trust checks. CVE-2026-123872 lets a client switch the server name during TLS 1.2 renegotiation. It can carry a normal login to a host that needs stricter client certificates. CVE-2026-123867 is a related per-host mutual TLS bypass. A host configured with only a CA falls back to the default CA, so the wrong client can get in. CVE-2026-123877 affects https.Agent . A cached TLS session from a broad trust policy can be reused by a request with a stricter policy. The second request then reports authorized === true when it should not. CVE-2026-126051 lets a remote client crash TLS servers that use hooks such as SNICallback or addContext() . CVE-2026-123871 prints proxy credentials inside ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG errors. That puts secrets into logs and crash reports. It repeats the lesson from CVE-2026-48615. The three low flaws touch the Permission Model and zlib. CVE-2026-123829 leaks file names on macOS and Windows. CVE-2026-106071 lets a wildcard grant match more paths than intended. CVE-2026-123862 can crash an app that calls deflate.params() while streaming, though that use is rare. Researcher Chris Rohlf, working with Claude and Anthropic Research, reported five of the 16 flaws. Other reporters include Pimterry, Trail of Bits, and several independent researchers. Matteo Collina fixed most of them. This release followed a short warning. Our earlier story on the scheduled patch noted that the notice gave no CVE details. The full list is now public. October’s Node2Shell Brotli bug and July’s 11 fixes show that Node.js ships serious fixes almost every month. Upgrade to v22.23.5, v24.22.3, or v26.13.1 first. Public HTTP/2 and HTTPS servers should go first. Then rebuild container images so they carry the new runtime. Teams that served traffic from a vulnerable HTTPS handler should consider replacing their TLS keys, since leaked memory leaves no clear trace. End-of-life versions are always affected, so move off them. The Node.js release schedule lists support dates. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Smashing Security podcast #492: How hackers turned Russian cars into pumpkins
items.summary: You're driving your new Chinese SUV when the dashboard goes dark. Ten minutes later, your phone rings. A stranger says they've got the digital key to your car, and would you like it back? Of course you would. That'll be $550. Meanwhile, three men have been charged over a scheme that used deepfakes of company bosses to steal around $130 million. Hear more about what happened, and the simple human trick that can foil the fakes. All this and more in episode 492 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Danny Palmer.
